summary: One of two FYI documents collecting the most commonly asked questions from new Internet users, with answers. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 2664.

eli5.summary: A list of questions beginners often ask, with answers, like a welcome guide for a new school. A newer guide replaced it.

questions: what is the difference between rfc and std
subtitle: A 1994 beginner's FAQ for the Internet: what it is, where documents live, which services exist and how to use them.

tldr.problem: New Internet users all ask the same basic questions, and answers were scattered or unwritten.
tldr.mechanism: The User Services Working Group collected the most common questions with short answers, grouped into topics such as the Internet, DNS, RFCs, organizations, services, mailing lists and Internet lore, plus a condensed glossary.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational and sets no standard. It is obsoleted by RFC 2664 and replaced RFC 1325, and it is a snapshot of how the Internet looked in March 1994.

today: RFC 1594 is Informational and is obsoleted by RFC 2664. It obsoleted RFC 1325. Its contacts, addresses and service descriptions date from March 1994, so it is mainly of historical interest.

sections.title: What This FYI Is
sections.content:
RFC 1594 is FYI 4, one of two FYI documents called Questions and Answers produced by the IETF User Services Working Group. The goal is to document the most commonly asked questions and answers on the Internet. It is informational and specifies no Internet standard of any kind.

The RFC number will change with each update, but the designation FYI 4 will not. A companion, FYI 7, covers intermediate and advanced topics. This edition obsoletes RFC 1325 and adds new questions on the InterNIC, gopher, the World Wide Web and Mosaic, and other resource discovery tools.
sections.eli5: It is a list of questions beginners ask, with answers. The same guide gets new editions over the years but keeps the same label, FYI 4.

sections.title: The Internet, TCP/IP and DNS
sections.content:
The Internet is described as a collection of thousands of networks linked by a common set of technical protocols, TCP/IP. It started with the ARPANET and by then included networks such as NSFNET, AARNet, NASA Science Internet and SWITCH, among about 10,000 others. Networks not built on TCP/IP can still exchange email through mail gateways.

TCP/IP is called a family of over 100 data-communications protocols. Beyond TCP and IP, the main protocols named are SMTP, FTP and TELNET. The Domain Name System is described as a hierarchical, distributed method of organizing the name space, which removes dependence on a centrally maintained file mapping host names to addresses. A fully qualified domain name, such as atlas.arc.nasa.gov, includes all higher level domains up to the top level.

The text also says that getting a list of all Internet hosts is not useful: the list had more than 1.5 million hosts, almost all requiring access permission.
sections.eli5: The Internet is many smaller networks that all agree to speak the same language. Names like atlas.arc.nasa.gov work like an address that gets more specific from right to left.

sections.title: RFCs, FYIs, STDs and Drafts
sections.content:
This part explains the document series. RFCs are working notes of the Internet research and development community. They are not refereed publications, but they get technical review. Most standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards. Once published, an RFC is never revised or reissued under the same number, though a protocol can be re-documented in several RFCs. The reference for current status is RFC 1540, "Internet Official Protocol Standards".

An FYI (For Your Information) is a subset of RFCs aimed at a wide audience and keeps its FYI number even if reissued under a new RFC number. An STD number goes only to specifications that completed the full standardization process, and stays fixed too. For example, the Domain Name System is specified by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, both labeled STD 13.

It also covers how to obtain RFCs (anonymous FTP, email servers, and the email-based RFC-INFO service), the Internet Monthly Report, and Internet Drafts, which are working documents of the IETF and are not RFCs.
sections.eli5: RFCs are the Internet's public notebooks. Some notebooks are rule books (standards) and some are just helpful notes like this one.

sections.title: Internet Organizations and Contacts
sections.content:
The guide lists who does what. The IAB (Internet Architecture Board) handles technical and policy issues of the Internet architecture, reviews standards and manages RFC publication. Under it, the IETF coordinates operation and evolution, run by its chair and the IESG, and the IRTF promotes research. The Internet Society is a non-profit that was integrating the IAB, IETF and IRTF functions.

The IANA coordinates the assignment of protocol parameter values, which are documented in the Assigned Numbers RFC. The InterNIC is described as a five year project, partly supported by the National Science Foundation, that began operations in April 1993 and was split among three organizations for information, directory and registration services. The text also explains NIC and NOC, the older DDN NIC, and the Internet Registry (IR).
sections.eli5: Different groups play different roles, like a school with a principal, teachers, a research club and an office that hands out locker numbers.

sections.title: Services of the Early 1990s
sections.content:
The services section is a tour of what a new user could do in 1994. It covers finding email addresses with WHOIS, the Knowbot Information Service and PSI's White Pages. It explains USENET and Netnews (a distributed news service with no central administration) and newsgroups, of which there were approximately 900. It covers anonymous FTP, with the username anonymous and your email address as password.

It also describes archie, which tracked anonymous FTP archives (some 2,100,000 files at some 1,000 sites, with 22 servers listed), gopher, a menu-driven information browser from the University of Minnesota, and the World Wide Web, a hypermedia browser whose most familiar clients were the Mosaic programs from NCSA. TELNET is explained as remote login.

Mailing list advice stresses sending subscription requests to the administrative address, such as a -request mailbox, not to the list. It also gives address conventions for sending mail to BITNET, UUCP, SprintMail, CompuServe and MCIMail.
sections.eli5: It shows beginners how to find people, join discussion boards, grab free files and browse information, using the tools that existed back then.

sections.title: Internet Lore, Glossary and Status
sections.content:
The "Internet lore" part explains smileys such as :-), abbreviations like btw, fyi, imho, wrt and rtfm, and the FAQ list posted to news.announce.newusers. The RFC ends with suggested reading, a reference list and a condensed glossary of Internet terms. Its Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed.

Because it is a Q/A list for newcomers, many tools and addresses it names reflect early 1994. Treat it as history, not as current instructions.
sections.eli5: It ends with fun notes, like how to make a sideways smiley, and a mini dictionary of Internet words.
